mcqs.question: What does splitting instruction execution into multiple shorter cycles allow a multi-cycle datapath to do that single-cycle can't?
options: Execute two instructions simultaneously on the same hardware
Reuse the same ALU and memory port across different steps of an instruction, instead of needing duplicate hardware
Skip the decode stage for simple instructions entirely
Run at a slower overall clock frequency with no other benefit
mcqs.explanation: Because steps are separated in time, one ALU can serve both address calculation and arithmetic, and one memory port can serve both fetch and data access. This isn't simultaneous execution of two instructions (that's pipelining/superscalar), decode still happens for every instruction, and the design's benefit is hardware reuse, not merely a slower clock.

mcqs.question: Why does a register-register add typically take fewer cycles than a load in a multi-cycle datapath?
options: Loads are always executed twice for correctness
The ALU runs faster specifically for add instructions
The add instruction skips the memory-access cycle since it doesn't need to touch memory
The register file is slower to access than memory
mcqs.explanation: Add has no memory step, so its cycle count is naturally shorter (e.g., 4 vs 5 cycles) — the core efficiency win multi-cycle design recovers. The ALU's speed doesn't vary by instruction type, loads aren't executed twice, and register file access is generally faster than memory, not slower.

mcqs.question: What determines the exact sequence of states an FSM controller steps through for a given instruction?
options: The clock frequency of the CPU
The amount of available cache memory
A random selection made each cycle
The instruction type being processed, since different instructions need different steps
mcqs.explanation: The FSM's state sequence depends on the instruction currently in progress — a load takes a different path through states than an add. Clock frequency affects timing, not the sequence itself, the sequence is deterministic (not random), and cache size is unrelated to FSM state transitions.

mcqs.question: What's the key difference between multi-cycle design and pipelining, given both aim to improve on single-cycle inefficiency?
options: Multi-cycle processes one instruction at a time across several cycles; pipelining overlaps multiple instructions in different stages simultaneously
Multi-cycle overlaps multiple instructions; pipelining processes one instruction at a time
They are functionally identical approaches with different names
Pipelining shares hardware across steps, while multi-cycle duplicates it per stage
mcqs.explanation: Multi-cycle still finishes one instruction before meaningfully starting the next's steps; pipelining keeps several instructions in flight at once across stages. They aren't identical (throughput differs substantially), and it's multi-cycle that reuses shared hardware, while pipelining typically duplicates resources per stage — the reverse of what's suggested.

mcqs.question: Why does a branch instruction take fewer cycles than a load in this multi-cycle datapath?
options: Branches skip the memory-access cycle (no data memory touched) and the write-back cycle (they update the PC, not a general-purpose register), while loads need both
Branches are executed by a completely separate, faster ALU
Branches always execute in exactly one cycle regardless of datapath design
The FSM controller treats branches as a special case that skips the fetch cycle
mcqs.explanation: A branch's own work (compare two registers, compute a target) needs no data-memory access and writes the PC instead of the register file, so it naturally skips two of load's five steps — 3 cycles versus load's 5. There's no separate ALU for branches, cycle count is very datapath-dependent (not a universal one-cycle constant), and fetch is never skipped — every instruction needs it.

mcqs.question: Why can a multi-cycle design outperform a single-cycle design on simple instructions, even though those instructions now take multiple cycles instead of one?
options: Because single-cycle's one cycle must be as long as the slowest whole instruction (usually load), while multi-cycle's clock period only needs to fit the slowest single step — so a simple instruction's several short cycles can add up to less total time than one long single-cycle period
Because multi-cycle designs run at a fundamentally higher clock frequency for unrelated reasons
Because multi-cycle designs skip the fetch step for simple instructions
Cycle count alone determines total time, so multi-cycle can never actually be faster
mcqs.explanation: The real comparison is cycle length x cycle count, not cycle count alone: single-cycle's long period is sized for the worst-case instruction, while multi-cycle's short period only needs to cover the worst-case single step, so simple instructions finish in several short periods that can sum to less time than one long single-cycle period. Clock frequency differences aren't the mechanism, fetch is never skipped, and cycle count alone is exactly the wrong metric to compare on.
